## External, Integrated and Digital PersonalizaƟon: How the Mobile Phone Became Unique

mobile phones, personalizaƟon, customizaƟon, digital culture

Markku Reunanen markku.reunanen [a] aalto.fi Senior university lecturer, Aalto University Docent, University of Turku

Adela Lujza Lučenič lujza.lucenicova [a] aalto.fi MA student, Aalto University

Petra Noppari petra.noppari [a] aalto.fi MA student, Aalto University MSc student, Tampere University

Lu Chen lu.1.chen [a] aalto.fi MA student, Aalto University

How to cite: Reunanen, Markku, Adela Lujza Lučenič, Petra Noppari & Lu Chen. 2025. ”External, Integrated and Digital PersonalizaƟon: How the Mobile Phone Became Unique”. WiderScreen Ajankohtaista. hƩps://widerscreen.fi/numerot/ajankohtaista/external-integrated-and-digital personalizaƟon-how-the-mobile-phone-became-unique/

This arƟcle examines the development of mobile phone personalizaƟon from the mid-1990s to the early 2000s, focusing on three key categories: external, integrated and digital personalizaƟon. As mobile phones evolved from uƟlitarian devices to personal accessories, a wide range of stakeholders introduced opƟons for consumers to personalize their devices. Phone cases, colorful covers, ringtones and operator logos gave birth to a complete industry supporƟng such customizaƟon. Drawing on two main sources, contemporary magazines and newspapers, and unforeseen material from the recently opened Nokia Design Archive, we use Madeleine Akrich’s concepts of script and projected user to analyze how these stakeholders shaped mobile phone personalizaƟon. More than surface-level decoraƟon, such modificaƟons became a key mechanism for technology adopƟon, individual disƟncƟon and cultural integraƟon of mobile technology at the turn of the millennium, reflecƟng shiŌs in consumer idenƟty, design pracƟces and the emerging mobile media culture.

## IntroducƟon

The 1990s were a decade of rapid growth for the mobile phone industry. Even if exisƟng technologies, such as the Nordic NMT and American AMPS, had already earlier facilitated car and hand-held phones, it was over the 1990s that the mobile phone became affordable and personal, when companies started increasingly targeƟng the mass market (e.g. Häikiö 2001, 17, 178). In addiƟon to technical development, the shiŌ required effort for changing the mobile phone’s professional – even yuppie – image into something that would appeal to wider audiences (e.g. Haddon 1997; Pantzar 2000, 109–11). One factor that went firmly hand in hand with such efforts was personalizaƟon, which manifested itself in a number of ways ranging from colorful covers to ringtones and so-called operator logos. In this arƟcle, we chart the kinds of personalizaƟon opƟons that were available to customers in the 1990s and early 2000s, the roots of such opƟons, and the stakeholders involved in providing and facilitaƟng them. Another closely related term, customizaƟon, can be thought to include personalizaƟon, but also technical features, such as supported networks, storage size, memory capacity and camera specificaƟons, which are not uniform across markets even if the base device is (e.g. Comstock, Johansen & Winroth 2004; Choe, Liao & Sun 2012). The framing here could be defined as Nokia and Finland first, with comparisons to others, as the company was the market

leader since 1998 (Häikiö 2001, 177) and, arguably, also the design leader of the Ɵme, who 
introduced or popularized several personalizaƟon features. DisƟlled into two research quesƟons: 
 How did mobile phone personalizaƟon emerge, evolve and become integrated into 
consumer culture during the late 1990s and early 2000s? 
 What roles did different stakeholders play in shaping this process? 
DomesƟcaƟon (Silverstone, Hirsch & Morley 1992) and diffusion of innovaƟons (Rogers 1962) are 
two common theories that have been applied to early mobile phone adopƟon (e.g. Haddon 1997; 
Jaakkola, Gabbouj & Neuvo 1998; Leung & Wei 1999; Lehtonen 2003; Koskinen & Kurvinen 2005). 
As per its name, domesƟcaƟon deals with the domesƟc sphere, which only parƟally matches the 
use cases of a mobile phone (see Silverstone 2006). All in all, a general model of technology 
adopƟon is not parƟcularly useful when focusing on devices’ low-level features. Diffusion is a 
somewhat beƩer candidate with its innovaƟon-decision process model and adopter categories, 
but not a direct match either, as our focus is not on the spread of technology in social networks. 
Madeleine Akrich’s (1992) concepts of script and projected user are a beƩer fit for the general 
analysis here because of our interest in designers’ expectaƟons about users’ tastes, skills, needs 
and moƟvaƟons. Furthermore, when creaƟng personalizaƟon opƟons, designers envision ways of 
how they will be used, or in other words they script the technological object. Akrich’s work is an 
extension of Actor-network theory and, therefore, naturally lends itself to the study of a diverse 
network of actors – be they people, insƟtuƟons or technologies. As we will demonstrate, early 
mobile phone personalizaƟon, too, came to be because of the interacƟons within such a network. 
The main bodies of research material for this arƟcle are newspaper and magazine arƟcles, 
adverƟsements and the diverse materials found in the Nokia Design Archive. Most of the arƟcles 
and adverƟsements were selected from the Finnish IltalehƟ tabloid, as it was in wide circulaƟon 
and represents what the general public saw at the Ɵme, not just special audiences. The search 
started with phone model names and the personalizaƟon opƟons we could iniƟally think of, 
expanded as we discovered more, and finished with 74 items when no new content appeared. As 
personalizaƟon is linked to fashion and trends, some addiƟonal searches to Vogue and Vanity Fair 
provided extra data on how phone companies tried to reach such audiences. The online Mobile 
Phone Museum (n.d.) was used for finding technical specificaƟons and publicaƟon years of phone 
models. 

The Nokia Design Archive (2025) is a collecƟon of the company’s documents and arƟfacts 
generated during their design processes. These materials were donated to Aalto University by 
MicrosoŌ Mobile oy and designers when the company ceased its phone producƟon business 
around 2016. For this research, the archive provided unique phone manufacturer’s perspecƟves 
with formerly confidenƟal materials, such as concept presentaƟons, sketches, and design research 
documents. All selected materials – 38 items from IltalehƟ, 14 from Vogue, 4 from Vanity Fair and 
13 from the Nokia Design Archive – were subjected to a close reading of both their textual and 
visual content to unearth details, such as stakeholders, argumentaƟon, proposed target audiences 
and properƟes of personalizaƟon opƟons (see BrummeƩ 2009). 
AŌer the introducƟon, we proceed to related work and provide an overview of how other 
researchers have studied mobile phone customizaƟon and personalizaƟon, followed by discussion 
on how fashion and trends shaped the device. Next follows an overview of our triparƟte typology 
of personalizaƟon, uƟlized in the following three secƟons where we provide examples of each 
category, coupled with discussion on their development before the smartphone age and the 
stakeholders involved. Finally, we provide some general conclusions concerning mobile phone 
personalizaƟon and its evoluƟon. 

## From a Tool to a Commodity

Mobile phone personalizaƟon has evolved in response to both technological improvements and shiŌing market demands. From the 1980s to the mid-1990s, mobile phones were generally bulky and uniform, with a focus on basic funcƟonality and connecƟvity for serving mainly business clients (e.g. Haddon 1997). An important evoluƟonary step was taken with the introducƟon of the GSM standard, first deployed in Finland in 1991, which enhanced network efficiency, compaƟbility and scalability, making mobile phones increasingly accessible to the general public. So-called feature phones were introduced in the early 2000s, along with mulƟmedia capabiliƟes, like MP3 players, FM radios, customizable ringtones, wallpapers and alarm sounds. A new stakeholder group became prominent as teleoperators began targeƟng a growing consumer market by offering mass customizaƟon opƟons for their products (Choe, Liao & Sun 2012). In their arƟcle, Choe, Liao and Sun (2012) discuss the challenges manufacturers faced when prioriƟzing mass customizaƟon possibiliƟes for the rapidly expanding consumer market at the Ɵme. According to their definiƟon, mass customizaƟon is the strategic middle ground that aims to

balance mass manufacturing and standardizaƟon with the manufacturer’s predetermined 
customizaƟon possibiliƟes. They underline that the mass customizaƟon of mobile phones includes 
both hardware and soŌware modificaƟons. PersonalizaƟon, according to them, occurs aŌer 
purchase and is driven by the consumer rather than the manufacturer. It is more individualized and 
frequently focuses on the interface and user experience rather than physical features. (ibid.) User 
experience here refers to how users engage with mobile phone customizaƟon features, the sense 
of joy and emoƟonal connecƟon they feel while personalizing their devices, and the overall 
convenience and intuiƟveness of using those customizaƟon opƟons. 
Whereas Choe, Liao and Sun’s (2012) paper acts as a pracƟcal link between theoreƟcal 
understanding and industrial applicaƟon by conducƟng empirical research on which customizaƟon 
features provide the most value, Blom and Monk (2003), and Häkkilä and Chaƞield (2006) seek to 
understand the customer moƟves that drive why and how users modify their devices. According to 
their research, users tweak their devices not just to improve their appearance, but also to 
represent their individuality, provide an improved user-friendly experience, and form emoƟonal 
Ɵes with their technology. Blom and Monk’s (2003) theoreƟcal study, and Häkkilä and Chaƞield’s 
(2006) empirical case study conclude that users gradually customize their gadgets over Ɵme, adjust 
seƫngs to different social contexts, and are moƟvated by both funcƟonal benefits and personal 
expression. 
Comstock, Johansen and Winroth (2004) summarize the transiƟons of the Swedish mobile phone 
industry and how companies may develop the ability to deliver customizaƟon at scale. According 
to their findings, significant improvements in both organizaƟonal procedures and supply chain 
interacƟons were required to facilitate mass customizaƟon, as well as closer integraƟon of design, 
manufacturing and distribuƟon systems. While Comstock, Johansen and Winroth (2004) present 
industrial perspecƟves on how manufacturers can provide mass customizaƟon opƟons, Choe, Liao 
and Sun (2012) detail the types of customizaƟon opƟons users prefer, Häkkilä and Chaƞield (2006) 
present a case study on user customizaƟon pracƟces, and Blom and Monk (2003) evaluate the 
psychological reasons why users want to customize and personalize their devices. CustomizaƟon is 
a mulƟfaceted trend that requires not only industrial experƟse but also an understanding of 
consumer preferences, habits and underlying reasons for personalizaƟon. To use Akrich’s (1992) 
terminology, the expectaƟons concerning the projected user are turned into a script embedded in 
the device itself and its surrounding material, such as adverƟsements and user manuals.
